en: Sūtra: The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas... up to the forty-eight minor precepts, which shall now be explained.
Commentary: From here below, the minor precepts are recited individually. This section contains three parts: first, concluding the previous section and introducing the subsequent one;

second, the sequential recitation of the precepts; and third, the conclusion with an exhortation to practice them. This is the first part. These various minor precepts, according to their respective...
One should understand the underlying intention, whether there is an offense or no offense, whether it is defiled or non-defiled, and whether it is weak, middling, or intense.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
among these, stained transgressions refer to those committed with a corrupt intention.
Not so. Even if there is an association with afflictions, it is called "non-defiled transgression," according to the three grades of distinction such as the state of mind and so forth.
As stated in the sixty-eighth [verse]:
"An offense becomes grave through six distinctions. First, that which is grave by virtue of being prescribed as such by the Teacher."
Second, the gravity of the matter;
third, the frequency of transgression;
fourth, the intensity of the afflictions.
Fifth, the power of wisdom is inferior;
sixth, one does not quickly repent.
Each of these various precepts fully possesses the meaning of the three clusters of precepts (tri-skandha-śīla).
The opening and closing of the various teachings varies according to necessity.
Regarding the forty-eight minor precepts: First is the Precept on Not Respecting Teachers and Elders. This is the first sutra.
"If a son of the Buddha wishes to accept the position of a king, or [any other such rank], if he does not do so [according to the prescribed method], he commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Commentary states:
From this point downward, the text is recited separately.
The first ten consist of fourteen gates.
The first two are the gates of guarding one's own mind through mindfulness;
they are established because arrogance and negligence are restrained at their respective points.
Because one severs the fault of intoxication regarding the grounds of negligence,
the next three [precepts] are the gate of conduct for protecting the minds of others,
and the subsequent three are the gate of aspiring to cultivate the Buddha-dharma.
The latter two are the gates for protecting sentient beings;
those who have previously received the precepts shall receive positions such as kingship.
There are two traditions regarding this.
One says that although the Bodhisattva had previously possessed precepts, [he lost them].
At that time, one further undertakes [the vow] for the sake of disciplining the mind;
although the non-informative [action] is induced by the presence of the manifest [action] and other conditions, [it arises through this further undertaking].
Because it belongs to the same category as the preceding precepts, it is said not to be newly acquired.
As stated in the Abhidharma:
"For one who has already produced roots of goodness based on nirvāṇa, they do not arise anew."
Is it not the case that at a later time, seeds are produced through perfuming?
This [case] should also be understood in the same way.
If there were never previously any precepts...
What is meant by "son of the Buddha"?
What minor offense has been committed?
Regarding this, some say:
Regarding the rules and procedures for the prātimokṣa precepts, as with the bhikṣu precepts, there is no method for receiving them again.
Even if one were to receive them repeatedly, it would merely augment the existing precepts.
Consequently, once a bodhisattva has entered the first stage (bhūmi), they relinquish the contaminated (sāsrava) precepts and receive the uncontaminated (anāsrava) precepts.
Because one wishes to nurture the qualities for attaining Buddhahood,
and because the precepts already exist [prior to this],
the Path of Seeing cannot be attained [at that stage].
Unlike the Śrāvakas, who attain the precepts upon reaching the Path of Vision because they previously lacked them,
the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that receiving them again does not constitute a new acquisition.
This differs from other dharmas, where seeds are repeatedly perfumed.
Because he does not establish formal laws or ritual regulations,
there is no fault in being a son of the Buddha even if one has not yet received the precepts,
provided that one has already made the aspiration for supreme enlightenment.
Regarding those who commit minor offenses:
they give rise to conceit;
is it not necessary for them to undergo severe retribution before their transgression is cleared?
If the mind had already been disciplined,
[the teaching] would be useless; therefore,
he is called the "Elder" (sthavira).
The "foremost among the assembly" refers to the *upādhyāya*, that is,
the Preceptor (*kalyāṇamitra*) who confers the precepts.
The *ācārya* is the preceptor (*śāstṛ*),
the teacher who imparts the ritual procedures for ordination (*karmavācanā*), the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*), the instructions for receiving [the precepts],

and the training in the duties thereof. Those who study together, hold the same views, and practice together are, respectively, those who share the same teacher, the same school, and the same vehicle.
As for what are called the seven treasures,
even those things held most precious can still be given as gifts.
How much more so for the remaining minor [offenses];
this is the intended meaning here.
To say "if it were not otherwise" means:
To pay respect and make offerings in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma is improper.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"It constitutes a defiled transgression when committed with a mind of pride, resentment, or anger."
Laziness and forgetfulness constitute an offense that is non-afflicted.
There is no transgression if one is ill, insane, or asleep.
Either preaching the Dharma oneself, or conversing with others, or listening to the Dharma oneself;
or wishing to protect the mind of the Dharma-preacher,
or for the sake of protecting the minds of many sentient beings.
Whether for the purpose of subduing [a person] or to protect the monastic regulations, there is no offense in either case. 2.
The Second Sūtra on the Precept Against Drinking Alcohol.
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally drinks alcohol, or even teaches others to drink it, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The commentary states:
Alcohol is the root from which delusion and confusion arise, and the source of all transgressions.
Formerly, this was the terrain for subduing dragons;
now it cannot restrain even the toads,
such that the four rebellious ones have arisen from this.
This is now established as a prohibition, with the sole exception of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
As for the statement that "the faults are immeasurable":
Because one incurs an offense only when committing a transgression while intoxicated;
as the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"There is no nature-offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) in the limited measure [of medicine] used for treating illness."
Therefore, it is known that this is a prohibitory offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Those who uphold the Vinaya say it is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Upāli asked, "How should I provide for the sick?
The World-Honored One said:
Except for those offenses that are transgressions by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*),
all [other requisites] may be provided; however, there was a member of the Śākya clan who was afflicted by a disease and required wine.
Because the Blessed One did not permit them to drink alcohol,
and because even noble ones (*ārya*) who have been reborn [in other realms] do not commit such an offense.
Thus say the masters of the Abhidharma.
It is not an intrinsic transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Nevertheless, for the sake of the sick, the prohibitions and permissions of the precepts were generally relaxed;
subsequently, at another time, the drinking of alcohol was prohibited.
This is to prevent the commission of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) by using it;
furthermore, all noble ones (*ārya*) do not drink alcohol because the noble ones possess a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
Because drinking it causes one to lose right mindfulness;
even a small amount must not be drunk,
for its dosage is as unpredictable as that of a poisonous drug.
Regarding the statement that for five hundred lifetimes one shall be handless:
this is due to the extreme intensity of the evil mind,
and not because of a wholesome mind or the like.
If it is a gift with a virtuous mind,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* allows that it is subsumed under the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*),
as stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*: [as follows].
A lay bodhisattva incurs no fault when giving alcohol.
They should give rise to this thought:
"The dharma of the perfection of giving fulfills all the wishes of people."
Because one should later employ skillful means to teach and transform others so that they abstain from alcohol,
it is said that one must not even instruct others [to drink], let alone drink it oneself.
This is first illustrated by using a vessel that has overflowed as a metaphor for having already drunk it oneself.
This is the second [case], which uses the act of instructing others to drink as an illustration for drinking oneself.
If one intentionally drinks it oneself or instructs others to drink it,
this constitutes a summary transgression.
However, the Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra states:
"One must not drink alcohol.

If it is for medicinal purposes as prescribed by a physician, where many medicinal ingredients are blended together, it is permissible to use [alcohol] provided that the medicine is predominant and the alcohol is minimal."
One must not consume oil nor apply it to the body and so forth;
however, if there is a specific cause or necessity, its use is permitted.
One may use milk, curd, fresh butter, and clarified butter.
I previously consumed milk gruel because of wind, phlegm, and cold.
In the *Adbhutadharma* (Sutra on Unprecedented Events), the five precepts are regulated as follows:
"If there is one who drinks alcohol and thereby gives rise to a joyful mind and produces wholesome states..."
Drinking [alcohol] does not constitute a violation of the precepts,
as explained at length therein;
how much more so for the Bodhisattva precepts, which bring benefit and involve no transgression.
Just as Vimalakīrti entered the wine shops and was able to establish their resolve. 3.
The Third Sūtra on the Precept Against Eating Meat.
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat—even down to [the case of] intentionally eating it—they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The commentary states:
It is logically appropriate for a bodhisattva to sacrifice his own flesh to save the lives of others;
yet, by conversely eating the meat of others, he will inevitably lead to their slaughter.
Therefore, this is the established rule.
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* stipulates for bodhisattvas:
"If meat has been killed specifically for oneself, one must not eat it."
If the meat is already rotten like withered trees and shrubs,
one may eat it; if one wishes to consume the meat, one should recite this mantra three times.

*Tadyathā* (thus it is): *amogha amogha* (non-self, non-self); *aśvabhāva aśvabhāva* (no life-principle, no life-principle); *naśa naśa* (perish, perish); *dagdha dagdha* (burn, burn); *bhindu bhindu* (break, break); *saṃkāpātami* (the conditioned); *svāhā* (may there be the cessation of killing). Mañjuśrī addressed [the Buddha], saying: [Thus it is].
If it were permissible to eat meat,
why did [the Buddha] completely prohibit it in various sutras such as the *Kūrma-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
Because sentient beings lack the power of compassion and harbor intentions to kill,
for these reasons and conditions, I have prohibited the eating of meat.
Mañjuśrī, there are sentient beings who delight in wearing rag-robes.
I speak of the refuse-rag robe in this way;
begging for alms is likewise so.
For the sake of teaching and transforming them, I speak of the dhūta practices in this manner.
Mañjuśrī, because sentient beings harbor a mind of killing and harm, I have taught the abstention from meat. However,
if one can refrain from harboring a harmful mind and,
out of great compassion, acts for the sake of teaching and transforming all sentient beings, [meat may be consumed].
There is no fault. As for the statement that the seeds of the nature of great compassion are severed:
it is because of eating [meat] up to the point of killing.
Regarding the phrase "seeing him and departing":
when a hawk pursued it, the pigeon had not yet even ceased its terror at the shadow of Śāriputra,
let alone while standing in the place where food was being served.
Regarding the statement that eating meat incurs immeasurable transgressions,

this is as extensively revealed in the *Sarvajñāprabhasa-rṣi-amāṃsabhakṣaṇa-hetupratyaya-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions for the Rishi Sarvajñāprabhasa’s Abstention from Meat) concerning the faults of consuming it.
That rishi was none other than Maitreya.
When he attains Buddhahood, he will prohibit the eating of meat and establish it as a grave offense,
as fully described therein.
4. The Precept Against Eating the Five Pungent Herbs. Sutra on the Fourth Precept Regarding the Consumption of the Five Pungent Herbs:
"If a disciple of the Buddha does not eat the five pungent herbs—and yet intentionally eats them—they commit a minor offense."
The commentary states:
Although the five pungent vegetables are merely plants, they are foul-smelling and impure, making them difficult for the worthy and virtuous to approach; thus, they are avoided by the noble.
This is why it is prohibited.
Master Fazang said:
"Among these five types, 'large garlic' refers to the *gṛñjana*."
Some say that *jiǔcōng* (leeks) are *húcōng* (onions),
and *láncōng* (chives) are *jiācōng* (household onions).
The first three are common foods among humans:
*gé-cōng*. According to the *Erya*, it is the mountain leek (*shān-cōng*).
The stem is slender and the leaves are large;
it should be written as "ge" (茖),
and "ge" (革) is incorrect.
It exists in the northern regions but not in the south;
it is called *xingqu* (興渠),
and some say it is *yuntai* (芸臺).
However, I have not yet seen a textual source for this.
Some say that its leaves in the region south of the Yangtze River resemble those of wild garlic (*Allium*).
Its roots and stems resemble those of the leek (*allium fistulosum*);
it does not grow in the northern regions. Another explanation states: [text missing].
The Sanskrit name for the medicinal substance asafoetida is hiṅgu;
such is the traditional account.
Regarding these five pungent vegetables (pañcakaṣāya), one must not consume them except when they are necessary to treat one's own illness or when they provide some specific benefit.
As stated in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"One must not eat garlic;
however, if there is a specific cause or condition, one may eat it."
If one compiles these medicines to treat illness, they may be used.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that there are eighty thousand families of worms within my body, while the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states there are nine hundred million per family.
When my body is at ease and happy, they too are at ease and happy;
when my body suffers from hunger, they too suffer from hunger.
For this reason, whatever the Bodhisattva consumes, [he does so with such an intention].
All these are for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to those afflicted by *gū* (poisonous charms), so that they do not crave their taste.
5. The Fifth Sutra on Not Teaching the Confession of Precepts.
"If a disciple of the Buddha sees any sentient being and fails to cause them to repent their transgressions, they commit a minor offense (laghu-pāpaka).
Commentary states:
As it is said in the *Yogācārabhūmi*..."
A bodhisattva’s compassion for sentient beings who possess pure ethical discipline is not as great as that for those who transgress their precepts and thus turn toward the causes of suffering; yet,
if out of malice or resentment one abandons them through expedient means and fails to provide them with benefit, [one incurs a fault].
This is a defiled transgression.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"The afflictions of sentient beings are themselves the illness of the bodhisattva."
This is because the Bodhisattva’s failure to rescue others from suffering deeply violates the principle of providing benefit and happiness;
therefore, this rule is now established.
These eight precepts and others are all common to both the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva precepts.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) comprises the precepts of the seven classes of practitioners.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that one receives the eight precepts for the sake of the unsurpassed path.
As for those who speak of "violating the prohibitions":
The bhikṣu’s full precepts and the bodhisattva’s vows of restraint (saṃvara-śīla).
The seven heinous offenses are as follows. Regarding the eight unfavorable conditions (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa):
Some say there are eight states of non-leisure (*akṣaṇa*):

namely, birth in the three evil destinies, in the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*), as a long-lived deity, as one born blind, as one born deaf, as one who is clever and eloquent in worldly knowledge, in the time before a Buddha has appeared, and in the time after a Buddha has passed away.
Because these lack the opportunity to cultivate the path, they are called "non-leisure" and are also termed "difficulties."
That is an obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
Although it is not [an obstacle] to be confessed through formal confession (*pratideśanā*), it is nevertheless a case of designating the effect by the name of its cause.
Among these, the ten unwholesome actions bring about rebirth in the miserable realms;
worldly virtues lead to birth in the Northern Continent;
and wrong concentration results in a long life.
Those who slander the Dharma are born blind and deaf;
those with false wisdom attain clarity and discernment.
Those who do not revere the Triple Gem will experience birth after birth before and after the Buddhas.
Some say that among the thirteen difficult cases, the five heinous crimes (ānantarya) are excluded,
because those five are already included within the seven heinous crimes.
Although this is a general enumeration that includes cases such as those involving *duṣṭhūlā* offenses,
it is traditionally explained in this way.
As for the phrase "to commit a minor offense of defilement" (*laghu-pāpaka-apatti*):
Except when [the person] lacks the five virtues or, conversely, gives rise to faults;
in such cases, although one does not bring them to account, there is no transgression.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"There is no transgression if one understands that the person is incurable and cannot be spoken with."
If, considering the time, or considering that because of this there would be strife, litigation, and disorder among the community,
one knows that the person possesses intense shame and dread of blame and will return to purity.
If one does not reprimand, punish, or expel [the offender], there is no transgression in any of these cases. 6.
The Sixth Sūtra on Abiding in the Precept of Not Requesting the Dharma. Abiding in the Precept of Not Requesting the Dharma. The Sixth Scripture.
If a disciple of the Buddha sees a Mahāyāna Dharma Master and does not [respect him], he commits a minor offense (light defilement).
The commentary states:
That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
Because it can give rise to wisdom and realize nirvana,
the *Teaching Left Behind* (*Śāsanāntara*) states:
"Wisdom is the sturdy ship for crossing the ocean of birth and death."
A bright lamp for the dark night of ignorance;
an excellent medicine for all who are ill;
a sharp axe for felling the tree of afflictions.
Therefore, you should augment yourselves through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
It is the principle that Bodhisattvas should seek [the Dharma] even at the cost of sacrificing their bodies;
yet, to instead treat it with contempt and violate it is a profound transgression.
Therefore, this is the current regulation.
To speak of "monastic quarters" (saṅghārāma) refers to the system for those who have left the household life;
"houses" refer to those who remain at home.
This refers to cities, kings, and so forth.
"Three times each day" means at dawn,
at the time of the midday meal, and during the period when non-timely medicine is permitted.
As for those who consume three *liang* of gold daily,
they should not begrudge even the most precious treasures they hold dear. Why is this?
Because by giving non-noble wealth, one obtains noble wealth.
The distinction between these two types of wealth is as extensively detailed in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
One should constantly invite Dharma masters to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day.
If that Dharma teacher’s practice of wisdom is superior to one's own,
one should request them to preach the Dharma at the beginning, middle, and end of the day;
because of making such a request, one’s verbal karma is virtuous.
Because one pays homage at the three times, the bodily action is virtuous;
because one does not give rise to anger and so forth, the mental action is virtuous.
To speak for the sake of the Dharma and to request the Dharma by prostrating with the body—this is what is meant.
There are numerous instances, such as when one’s soul was nearly lost on the Snow Mountains while seeking even half a verse; there are also those who,
facing hardships such as illness, claim that others are inferior while they themselves are superior.
Not to comply when not requested.
7. The Seventh Scripture on the Precept Against Wandering for Study.
If a disciple of the Buddha sees [an opportunity] in any place—whether reaching it or not—and does not go there to listen and receive [the teaching], they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The commentary states:
The myriad practices converge in a single gateway;
this is what is meant by "attaining the meaning."
Acting with confidence, there is nothing that is not right.
Therefore, a novice bodhisattva who encounters matters without understanding their principle should travel and study in order to accomplish the practice of a sage.
As it is said in the sūtra:
"Even if the entire world were filled with fire,
one must pass through it in order to hear the Dharma."
One shall surely attain the Way of the Buddha and extensively deliver beings from the stream of birth and death.
The reason for this is as follows:
As stated in the Seventy-ninth [Chapter]:
"Unsurpassed enlightenment has wisdom as its essence;
wisdom is able to induce all the remaining perfections."
Therefore, when one engages in wrong conduct regarding wisdom,
it should be understood that the bodhisattva is engaging in wrong conduct toward both that awakening and the dharmas that lead to it.
For this reason, the bodhisattva holds the Dharma more lightly than the body.
Why is this? The verse says:
Wisdom regarding all virtuous practices.
Just as those supported by a boat and oars,
hundreds of thousands of blind people who have lost their way are preserved by means of a single eye.
Question: If that is so, why does a verse in the *Avataṃsaka* say:
"For example, like a poor person..."?
Day and night one counts another's treasures,
yet oneself has not even half a coin's share;
so it is with much learning.
The answer is that this merely negates the idea that hearing constitutes the ultimate goal;
it does not negate the noble wisdom rooted in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).
As a verse in the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
One who is learned is able to know the Dharma;
one who is learned is able to distance themselves from evil;
through learning, one abandons what is meaningless.
Through extensive learning, one attains nirvāṇa.
What is called *vinaya* is here translated as "subjugation."
Because it can cease the blazing evils of the three types of karma.
Regarding "listening to, receiving, and inquiring about [the teachings]," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice), fascicle 30, states:
A practitioner who has first begun their training, in order to realize the meaning and benefit [of the teachings],
should first establish right mindfulness in four places and then inquire.
What are these four places?
The summary verse says:
Without envy or pride,
and not for the sake of displaying one's own ability.
Having established the virtues of oneself and others,
one should then invite a Dharma master.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
To fail to go and listen and receive [the teaching] out of pride, resentment,
or anger constitutes a defiled transgression;
to do so out of laziness is a non-defiled transgression.
There is no offense if one is ill and lacks strength,
or if one knows that the teaching is being misstated.
Furthermore, having heard the number of teachings as they were explained,
one should either protect the mind of the speaker or diligently cultivate other virtues.
8. The Eighth Sūtra on the Precept of Turning One’s Back on the Right and Following the Deviant.
If a Buddha-son turns his heart away from the ultimate sūtras and vinaya, he commits a minor offense of defilement.
The commentary states:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says,
"Bodhisattvas fear the paths of the two vehicles."
Just as one who cherishes life fears the loss of the body,
so too does one who abandons the great for the small turn away from the bodhisattva path;
therefore, it must be restrained.
Question: If one turns their mind against the Mahāyāna and loses their precepts, how slight is this offense?
Answer: This constitutes a slander of the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddhayāna).
It is not because they have entirely turned their backs [on the Dharma].
That is to say, even if one does not possess faith or understanding, provided that on the Bodhisattva stage one does not slander [the teachings] but instead looks up to and honors the Tathāgata.
And there is no transgression.
As for the term "the eternally abiding sūtras and vinaya," it refers to that which is eternally abiding as the subject matter they expound.
The sūtras and vinayas are able to explain [the truth].
Furthermore, because the Buddhas of the three periods of time have taught the same and practiced the same without alteration,
if those of the two vehicles slander the emptiness of dharmas and so forth, it is termed wrong view.
9. The Precept on Not Attending to the Suffering of Illness. The Ninth Scripture on the Precept on Not Attending to the Suffering of Illness:
If a disciple of the Buddha sees anyone afflicted by illness and fails to provide relief, they commit a minor offense of defilement.
The commentary states:
The great compassion of a bodhisattva has the removal of suffering as its essential meaning.
There is no affliction more difficult to rescue than this illness.
Therefore, failing to provide relief constitutes a transgression,
because by attending to the sick, one bestows life itself.
To say that providing such care is no different from making offerings to the Buddha means:
The Buddha is the ultimate object of veneration;
illness is the ultimate object of compassion.
Although reverence and pity differ, their ultimate significance is the same.
Therefore, there is no difference.
Regarding the eight fields of merit, some say:
First, constructing beautiful wells in the wilderness;
second, building bridges over waterways;
third, leveling and clearing dangerous paths.
Fourth, serving one's parents with filial piety;
fifth, making offerings to śramaṇas;
sixth, making offerings to the sick.
Seventh, rescuing others from calamities and hardships.
Eighth, establishing the *amogha-pūjā* (unrestricted assembly). Regarding this, Master Fazang said:
"I have not seen this in the sacred teachings."

Now, let us explain. These are: first, the Buddha; second, the two types of noble ones (ārya); third, the upādhyāya; fourth, the ācārya; fifth, the Saṃgha; sixth, the father; seventh, the mother; and eighth, the sick person.
By what means is this known?
As the following text states: "The eight fields of merit consist of the Buddhas, the sages, each and every teacher and monk, one's parents, and the sick.
Regarding the statement "to commit a minor offense," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
If it is due to a mind of aversion or ill will, it is a defiled transgression;
if it is due to laziness, it is a non-defiled transgression;
there is no transgression in the following case.
If one is personally ill,
or lacks physical strength,
or requests another to act on one's behalf.
If one knows that the patient has someone to rely upon and someone to provide protection;
if one knows that the patient is personally capable of attending to their own needs;
and if one understands that the patient, though afflicted by a chronic illness, is able to sustain themselves.
If one is cultivating superior virtue so as to keep it uninterrupted;
if one knows oneself to be dull-witted and finds it difficult to cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom;
or if one has previously promised another to perform services for them.
Just as with a sick person,
one should know that it is likewise for those who are suffering and so forth; one acts as a companion in order to eliminate their suffering.
10. The Tenth Sūtra on the Precept Against Possessing Instruments of Killing.
If a disciple of the Buddha possesses anything down to knives or staves, they commit a minor secondary offense.
The commentary states:
A bodhisattva should accumulate things that benefit sentient beings;
to keep instruments of killing is a profound violation of compassionate salvation.
Therefore, it must be regulated.
Even regarding the killing of one's parents, no retaliation is to be meted out,
because it is the natural law of cause and effect that they themselves will experience the fruits of their own past karma.
One should not give way to anger;

The Seventh Scripture on Preaching the Dharma in Contravention of Ritual and Precepts.

If a disciple of the Buddha constantly engages in teaching and transforming others yet speaks in a manner that is not in accordance with the Dharma, they commit a minor offense (light defilement). Commentary states:
Respect for others and reverence for the Dharma give rise to supreme goodness;
otherwise, the opposite unwholesome qualities arise.
Among these, the wealthy and noble are singled out for mention because they are particularly prone to arrogance.
Regarding the phrase "those who listen," this refers to those seated below and others,
because they give rise to a sense of yearning and aspiration;
as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*:
If a person, though their footing of ethical discipline may be weak and inferior,
is able to preach the Dharma for the benefit of many people,
they should be honored as the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Because one accepts those teachings as being similar to the well-spoken Dharma.
Furthermore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"There are those who know the Dharma."
Whether old or young, they shall serve [the Buddha] as the gods of the Second Heaven serve Śakra.

"If a son of the Buddha, out of faith, should commit acts that destroy the Dharma, he incurs a secondary offense (light impurity). Commentary states:
If one does not allow an evil person to leave the household life,
